name: Benji
tagline: A consumer money app for tracking accounts, spending and recurring charges in one place.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The dashboard part of a personal finance app is genuinely easy: import transactions, categorize them, show monthly totals, flag things that repeat every 30 days. An agent will get you there in a sitting, and your rules will beat any generic categorizer because you know what "AMZN MKTP" actually was. The part you cannot one-shot is the bank connection, which means Plaid or a competitor, an application process, per-connection fees and a lifetime of institutions breaking their OAuth flows. Downloading CSVs once a month works fine and costs nothing, it just requires you to be the kind of person who downloads CSVs once a month.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app that ingests bank and card CSVs into SQLite, categorizes them with rules you write, and shows monthly spend plus detected recurring charges.
requirements: Node 20 and a local machine you trust with your transaction history
CSV exports from each bank or card you care about
optional: a Plaid developer account if you want real sync, plus patience
whatYouLose: Automatic bank sync, so your data is only as fresh as your last CSV download
A phone app that shows you a balance while you are standing in a store
Decent out of the box merchant naming and categorization, which is quietly a lot of curated data
Someone else worrying about credential storage, encryption and breach liability
Shared household views, alerts and any nudge that arrives when you are not already looking
moatNotes: The moat is not the charts, it is the aggregator contract, the merchant enrichment data and the security posture that makes people paste bank credentials at all.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the value of a money app is that it is already there when you open your phone, with clean merchant names and yesterday's transactions, without you doing anything. A local CSV dashboard delivers the same insight but demands a monthly chore, and personal finance tools die the moment they demand a chore. People pay a few dollars a month to outsource the ingestion problem and the discipline problem at once.
notes: The charts are a weekend; the freshness is not. Bank aggregation plus merchant enrichment is what you are actually renting.
prompt:
Build a local-only personal finance tracker. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry, no bank APIs.

Stack, not negotiable:
- Next.js with the App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/money.db
- Recharts for charts
- Runs with `npm run dev` on localhost only

Data model:
- accounts: id, name, type (checking, credit, savings)
- transactions: id, account_id, date, description, raw_description, amount (negative = spend), category, is_transfer, import_hash (unique)
- rules: id, pattern (case-insensitive substring or /regex/), category, priority

Features, in scope:
1. CSV import page: upload a file, pick the account, then map columns (date, description, amount) in a preview table. Support amount as one signed column or separate debit and credit columns. Dedupe on a hash of account + date + amount + raw_description.
2. Rules engine: apply rules in priority order on import and on demand via a "recategorize all" button. Uncategorized transactions land in "Uncategorized".
3. Transactions table: filter by month, account, category, and free text. Inline category edit. Editing a category offers "also create a rule for this description".
4. Dashboard: current month spend by category (bar), spend over the last 12 months (line), net cash flow, top 10 merchants. Exclude rows flagged is_transfer from all spend math.
5. Recurring detection: group by normalized description, flag groups with 3 or more charges at roughly 7, 14, 30 or 365 day intervals with similar amounts. List them with cadence, last charge and estimated annual cost.
6. Seed a starter rules file (groceries, rent, utilities, transport, restaurants, subscriptions) that I can edit as JSON.

Out of scope: Plaid or any aggregator, multi-user, budgets with rollover, investments, mobile app, auth.

Any secrets go in .env with a committed .env.example. Add ./data to .gitignore. Ship a README with a two-command setup, the CSV formats you tested, and a note that the database is unencrypted plain SQLite on my disk.
